2. You should involve information governance teams early in the project design process – this will help you to comply with privacy and data protection legislation, and plan resources effectively so that support is available for project teams when needed.

Your organisation’s data and information security team should be able to advise on security requirements and risks. 

Refer to the government’s [personal data security principles](https://www.gov.uk/guidance/principles-for-securing-personal-data-in-government-services) when processing and sharing personal data.

If you’re working with any third-party suppliers to store, collect or process data, make sure they’re vetted and that they comply with the security requirements of your project.

5. You should always follow your organisation’s internal governance policies
Data and AI projects should have appropriate and effective governance and oversight. This includes clear roles and responsibilities, clear documentation, and being transparent about the system and the processes around it.

6. You need strong oversight and clear responsibilities to ensure accountability across the life cycle of your project. You must set out who is responsible at each stage of the project.

This includes naming: senior responsible owners (SROs), data owners, data stewards, data custodians, and AI asset owners.

elements.name: 6aT

elements.name: 6aS

6a. As the primary risk owners for the project, senior responsible owners ensure a real policy or business need is being addressed, engage with stakeholders and assure ongoing viability. 
For project governance to be effective, it’s essential that the people accountable have appropriate technical expertise and knowledge, and authority, to implement necessary changes. This is especially important for complex projects or those involving multiple suppliers, which is often the case with data and AI projects.

7. To ensure AI and data projects can be audited or reviewed, your team must: record who is responsible for each part of the system, including suppliers, and record decisions made during project design, model deployment and system deployment processes.

For example, a data set factsheet can help explain how data was handled.
The [Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard (ATRS)](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/algorithmic-transparency-template) also provides a template for public sector organisations to document and share information about how and why they’re using algorithmic tools.

elements.name: 8a

elements.name: 8S
elements.title:
8. When designing a government tool or service, you should always start by learning about the people who will use it. If you don’t understand users or what they need from your service, you cannot build the right thing.

You should involve diverse stakeholders in the design and testing process and undertake thorough user research and public engagement to ensure you’re including the views of those that may be affected or digitally excluded.

You must understand and comply with your legal obligations and duties. Refer to the Public Sector Equality Duty (PSED) and the Equality Act 2010.

elements.name: 8aT
elements.title: 8a. Describe the measures you will take to protect research particpants.

elements.name: 8aS
elements.title:
8a. You must take steps to protect research participants. This applies to your team and to any third-party researchers you work with. 

You should:
o make sure that participants understand the research and any risks involved 
o only include participants who give clear, informed consent without pressure or coercion 
o allow participants to withdraw at any time (with exceptions for situations like medical research where participant information is anonymised and aggregated and cannot be removed from the research data set)
o anonymise all data used in reports or analysis.

The Service Manual has guidance on [managing user research data and participant privacy](https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/managing-user-research-data-participant-privacy).

elements.name: 8bT
elements.title: 8b. Describe the measures you will take to protect researchers.

elements.name: 8bS
elements.title:
8b. Some research projects involve sensitive topics, such as child protection or adult safeguarding. These can be distressing for both researchers and participants. To reduce risk, you should:
o highlight any sensitive topics in workshop or interview plans
o set up a ‘safety check-in’ protocol to support staff after sessions, particularly for one-to-one or lone working
o use existing ethical guidelines and processes, such as the Service Manual’s guidance on researching emotionally sensitive subjects

In rare cases, researchers may be targeted by participants or others. If this happens, or if the risk is known in advance, put safeguards in place to protect staff.

The Government Analysis Function provides a list of resources related to conducting research and analysis in government.

9a. Having a diverse and multidisciplinary team can provide a strong foundation for building fairer tools and services. A diverse team is often able to spot issues early in the development process by bringing varied perspectives and lived experiences.

If it’s not possible to assemble a diverse team, you should note any potential gaps in understanding and proactively seek ways to engage with a variety of stakeholders. This might include through user testing, public engagement and, where possible, presenting ideas at internal or external community events.

The Service Manual includes guidance on the [people you need to have in your team at each phase](https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/the-team/set-up-a-service-team).

o your project has a clear purpose
o there’s a clear public benefit

You should continually revisit user needs throughout your project. The Service Manual explains more about [user needs](https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/start-by-learning-user-needs).

11. You should include stakeholder perspectives by engaging with civil society groups, affected communities and wider public sector to understand values and impacts.

Proactive public and stakeholder engagement is critical to understand the potential impacts of a tool or system. Engaging with stakeholders can help to build trust and improve adoption of AI tools and systems.

Ethical use of data and AI means listening to different perspectives and checking that your tools work as intended. Otherwise, you could unintentionally exclude people or cause harm.

13. Have you considered the potential environmental impact and sustainability of your project?

elements.name: 13a
elements.title: 13a. Will you monitor, evaluate and address environmental impact and sustainability challenges throughout the project lifecycle?

elements.name: 13T
elements.title: 13. Briefly explain the environmental and sustainability implications of your project.

elements.name: 13S
elements.title:
13. Environmental sustainability means thinking about the wider impact of your project on people and the planet. It’s important to consider this from the start, as it can influence your choices about tools, suppliers and infrastructure.

The environmental sustainability chapter in the Data and AI Ethics Framework provides further advice on how to assess the potential impact of data and AI projects.

elements.name: 13aT
elements.title: 13a. Briefly describe how you intend to monitor, evaluate and address environmental impact and sustainability challenges.

elements.name: 13aS
elements.title:
13a. Before you begin building a tool or system, you should develop a plan to monitor and evaluate the environmental impact.

You should think about factors such as: 
o Whether AI is the best technology or tool for the task – there may be alternatives that provide as good, or better, results and require less resource-intensive training and development.
o Project size and complexity – how much data will be processed, the number of end users, bandwidth and latency requirements, prompt efficiency
o Software requirements – including model type.
o Hardware requirements – such as data centre usage or Internet of Things (IoT) devices.

The Service Manual also has guidance on how to build more [environmentally sustainable digital services in government](https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/design/environmentally-sustainable-services).
